### Observed differences

- Resource allocation changed on six activities. In the earlier window, A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22 were each handled by a stable group of resources, with the largest single shares around 10–12 assignments in 100 (User_18 held about 11 in 100 on A01 and A03). In the later window, a largely different group took over: User_35 and User_15, which held no listed share before, each handled roughly 8–11 assignments in 100 on all six activities, while User_18 fell to about 4–5 in 100 and several other previously prominent resources dropped out of the leading group entirely. The same gainers and losers recur on every one of the six activities. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- Work on A08 and A11 became more concentrated: the top resource's share rose from about 13 to about 27 assignments in 100, the number of distinct resources fell from 18 to 14, and the concentration index roughly doubled (about 0.08 to 0.14), on about 100 supporting traces per window. The two items carry identical profiles, so they may reflect one underlying behaviour rather than two independent confirmations. [CONC001, CONC002]
- The elapsed time between consecutive completions of A04 and A01 decreased: the mean fell from about 48 to about 24 hours, the median from about 32 to about 25 hours, and the spread narrowed (standard deviation about 71 to 31 hours), based on 200 completion gaps in each window; the difference exceeds about 999.5 of 1,000 random re-splits. [TWAIT001]
- No control-flow indicator qualified (0 items against about 0.16 expected without change), so activity participation and path usage show no qualifying difference; the qualifying differences are confined to resource allocation and timing. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, CONC001, CONC002, TWAIT001]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the possibility that work was reallocated across resources. On A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22, assignments moved from a previously dominant group of resources to a largely different one — User_35 and User_15 rose from little or no share to roughly 8–11 assignments in 100 each, while User_18 fell from about 10–11 to about 4–5 in 100 — and on A08 and A11 execution concentrated onto fewer resources, with the top resource's share roughly doubling. This is unlikely to be a sampling artefact: the resource family produced eight qualifying items where about 0.01 would be expected without change, the same gainers and losers recur across all six assignment profiles, and every difference is larger than in about 999.5 of 1,000 random re-splits. Participation counts per activity are similar in both windows (for example, 263 supporting observations before and after for A13 and A14) and no control-flow items qualified, so the change lies in who performs the activities, not in whether or how often they run. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, CONC001, CONC002]

Limitations: the resource codes are anonymous, so no roles, people or teams can be inferred; ASSIGN003/ASSIGN004 and CONC001/CONC002 carry identical profiles and are not independent confirmations. An important competing explanation the evidence cannot rule out is a change in the resource pool itself — new resources absorbing work as others withdraw — rather than an active reassignment of tasks; both would produce the same assignment profiles. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, CONC001, CONC002]

Other differences: the elapsed time between consecutive completions of A04 and A01 roughly halved on average (about 48 to 24 hours; median about 32 to 25 hours). As the only time item, against roughly 0.02 expected by chance for the time family, it is within what an unchanged process occasionally produces on its own, and the evidence cannot establish whether it is connected to the reallocation or independent of it. [TWAIT001]
